section.title: Envoys from Babylon
section.sectionRationale: This short chapter closes the Hezekiah narrative interlude, chapters 36 to 39, with a pivotal turn: Hezekiah's proud display of his treasures to Babylonian envoys draws Isaiah's prophecy that everything, and some of the king's own descendants, will one day be carried off to Babylon. This is the hinge that sets up the entire Book of Comfort, opening in chapter 40, addressed to a people who will indeed go into exile.
section.thesis: Hezekiah's proud display of his treasures to envoys from Babylon draws the prophecy that this same Babylon will one day carry everything away, revealing that even a good king's private pride can open the door to national consequence, and that God's coming word of judgment is also, already, the seed of the coming word of comfort.
section.frameNote: Three movements: Babylonian envoys arrive and Hezekiah shows them everything; Isaiah's probing question about what they saw; and the word of coming exile to Babylon, met by Hezekiah's ambiguous relief that peace will last in his own lifetime.

verses.text: At that time Merodach-baladan son of Baladan king of Babylon sent letters and a gift to Hezekiah, for he had heard about Hezekiah's illness and recovery.

And Hezekiah welcomed the envoys gladly and showed them what was in his {{otsar|treasure house}}, the silver, the gold, the spices, and the precious oil, as well as his entire armory, all that was found in his storehouses. There was nothing in his palace or in all his dominion that Hezekiah did not show them.

units.label: Isaiah's question
units.note: what have they seen in your palace

verses.text: Then the prophet Isaiah went to King Hezekiah and asked, “Where did those men come from, and what did they say to you?” “They came to me from a distant land,” Hezekiah replied, “from Babylon.”
“What have they seen in your palace?” Isaiah asked. “They have seen everything in my palace,” answered Hezekiah. “There is nothing among my treasures that I did not show them.”

units.label: The word of coming exile
units.note: at least there will be peace in my lifetime

verses.text: Then Isaiah said to Hezekiah, “Hear the word of the LORD of Hosts:
The time will surely come when everything in your palace and all that your fathers have stored up until this day will be carried off to Babylon. Nothing will be left, says the LORD.
And some of your descendants, your own flesh and blood, will be taken away to be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon.”
But Hezekiah said to Isaiah, “The word of the LORD that you have spoken is good.” For he thought, “At least there will be {{shalom|peace}} and security in my lifetime.”

otsar.gloss: Treasure house, storehouse, treasury. Hezekiah's eagerness to display every item in his otsar to foreign envoys, holding nothing back, becomes the very detail Isaiah singles out as the seed of coming judgment, since everything shown so proudly will one day be carried off exactly as displayed.

shalom.gloss: Peace, wholeness, security. Hezekiah clings to the thought that there will be shalom in his own lifetime even after hearing that his descendants will be exiled, a response that has troubled readers for centuries, since true shalom in Scripture usually includes concern for those who come after us, not comfort limited to our own days.

basic.context: Babylonian envoys arrive to congratulate Hezekiah on his recovery from illness, and Hezekiah, flattered by their attention, shows them every treasure in his kingdom, holding nothing back. Isaiah confronts him with a probing question, then delivers a hard prophecy: everything Hezekiah displayed, and some of his own descendants, will one day be carried off to Babylon, the very nation Hezekiah just entertained.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a real historical episode, also recorded in 2 Kings 20:12-19, that functions as a hinge in Isaiah's book: the same Babylon Hezekiah welcomes here will become the empire that later exiles Judah, the crisis the Book of Comfort, beginning in chapter 40, directly addresses. Hezekiah's final response, verse 8, has long been debated: is it humble acceptance of just judgment, or self-centered relief that trouble is deferred to future generations?
basic.originalLanguages: Hezekiah proudly displays everything in his {{otsar}}, treasure house, holding nothing back from foreign eyes, and this very openness becomes the detail Isaiah singles out as the seed of coming loss. Hezekiah's closing thought clings to {{shalom}}, peace, but only for his own lifetime, a response that reads as either resigned humility or troubling self-concern, depending on how it is read.
basic.typology: The prophecy that Hezekiah's own descendants will become eunuchs in Babylon's palace is later fulfilled, at least in principle, in figures like Daniel and his companions, who serve faithfully even in exile, showing that God's people can remain devoted to Him even under judgment's consequences. The movement from this chapter's judgment to chapter 40's comfort anticipates the gospel pattern of law exposing sin before grace announces good news.
basic.christ: This chapter's prophecy of exile is the very crisis the Book of Comfort answers, beginning with 'Comfort, comfort My people,' Isaiah 40:1, a comfort ultimately secured not by returning treasures but by Christ, who bears the judgment His people deserved so that a far greater and final comfort could be announced. The pattern here, judgment first, then Isaiah's turn to comfort, mirrors the gospel's shape: the law exposes sin before grace announces its remedy in Christ.
basic.god: God is not impressed by displayed wealth and does not let even a faithful king's pride go unaddressed, yet even in pronouncing judgment He is already planning the far greater comfort that will follow in the chapters ahead. His justice and His mercy are never separated; the same God who announces exile is the God preparing to comfort His people through it.
basic.crossReferences: 2 Kings 20:12-19 records the same episode in nearly identical language. 2 Chronicles 32:25-26 notes Hezekiah's pride after his healing and his subsequent humbling. Daniel 1:1-7 shows the beginning fulfillment of this prophecy, as young men of Judah's royal line serve in Babylon's palace. Isaiah 40:1 opens the comfort this chapter's judgment makes necessary.
basic.oneStory: This short episode shows how even a good king's private pride can open the door to national consequence, and how God's announcement of judgment is never His last word. The exile foretold here becomes the very crisis that the rest of Isaiah's book, and ultimately Christ Himself, answers with comfort, redemption, and a far greater homecoming than Hezekiah could have imagined.

context.literary:
The chapter is eight verses long and has the shape of a short play: an arrival, two questions, a verdict, a reply. What makes it work is the way each speech mirrors the one before.

The first scene is told with almost no comment. Merodach-baladan 'sent letters and a gift,' Hezekiah 'welcomed the envoys gladly,' and then comes a sentence that works like a list: silver, gold, spices, oil, armory, storehouses, and finally 'nothing in his palace or in all his dominion that Hezekiah did not show them.' The narrator exhausts the inventory and then says it again in the negative, so that completeness is the point.

In the second scene Isaiah asks two questions, and the king's answers repeat the vocabulary of the first scene. 'What have they seen?' draws out 'They have seen everything... nothing... that I did not show them,' which echoes the end of verse 2. Isaiah never accuses. He lets the king hear himself.

The third scene opens with a formal call to attention, 'Hear the word of the LORD of Hosts.' Everything the king displayed is now announced as being 'carried off,' and again the word 'nothing' returns, this time as 'Nothing will be left.' What the king had given away in a gesture is taken in a sentence. The final line is the king's, and it is the only unfiltered glimpse of his mind: his stated reply, 'good,' and his unspoken thought, 'peace and security in my lifetime.' The narrator does not tell us what to make of it.

The chapter is also a hinge in the book. Assyria looms over the earlier chapters, and chapters 40 to 55 will be spoken to a people in Babylon's shadow. Chapters 36 to 39 are the join. The name 'Babylon' runs through these few verses, and the chapter is the last prose before the poetry of comfort begins.
context.historical:
Merodach-baladan is the Hebrew form of the Babylonian name Marduk-apla-iddina, which means roughly 'Marduk has given an heir.' He was a Chaldean chieftain who took the throne of Babylon and defied the Assyrian kings for years. Assyrian records tell of Sennacherib defeating him early in his reign. His letters and gift to Hezekiah therefore come from a ruler who needed allies against Assyria.

The Bible gives two reasons the embassy came. Isaiah 39:1 and 2 Kings 20:12 say it was because Merodach-baladan heard Hezekiah had been ill and had recovered. Chronicles adds that the ambassadors came 'to inquire about the wonder that had happened in the land,' 2 Chronicles 32:31, probably the shadow that went back. The political motive, a military partnership, is not stated but is reasonable. The Hebrew word for his 'gift' is also used elsewhere for tribute, so the exchange may have carried some diplomatic weight on both sides.

The things Hezekiah showed are the realities of an ancient state. Silver, gold, spices and oil are portable wealth; the armory is military strength; the 'storehouses' (2 Chronicles 32:27 to 29 lists treasuries, grain stores and flocks) are what makes a siege survivable. A foreign power that has seen all of this knows both what is worth taking and how it is defended.

It also matters what Hezekiah had just lived through. He had stripped the temple doors and handed over every scrap of silver to Sennacherib in a desperate bid to buy him off, 2 Kings 18:14 to 16. His storehouses were full again, as 2 Chronicles 32:27 to 29 reports. The man who had been forced to empty them was proud to show them full.

The prophecy of verses 6 and 7 came true roughly a century later. Nebuchadnezzar 'carried off all the treasures from the house of the LORD and the royal palace,' 2 Kings 24:13, and at the final fall of Jerusalem the Chaldeans took the temple bronze and everything of gold and silver, 2 Kings 25:13 to 15. Royal young men, Daniel among them, were taken to the palace to be trained, Daniel 1:3 to 6.
context.canonical:
The story is told almost word for word in 2 Kings 20:12 to 19, with a significant addition in Chronicles. There, the story is a test: 'God left him alone to test him, that He might know all that was in Hezekiah's heart,' 2 Chronicles 32:31. Chronicles also says that his heart was proud and wrath came on Judah, until he and the people humbled themselves, 2 Chronicles 32:25 and 26. Together the three accounts present a king who passed through the great Assyrian trial and then stumbled over a courtesy.

The prophecy of verses 6 and 7 is a hinge for much of what follows in Scripture. Its fulfilment is described in 2 Kings 24 and 25, and in 2 Chronicles 36:18 to 20, with Jeremiah as its interpreter, 'When Babylon's seventy years are complete, I will attend to you,' Jeremiah 29:10. The Psalmist's 'By the rivers of Babylon we sat and wept,' Psalm 137:1, is the song of the people Isaiah saw coming.

It has older echoes too. A king who displays his treasure to a distant ruler is a type of what Deuteronomy warned against: kings who 'accumulate for himself large amounts of silver and gold,' Deuteronomy 17:17, and peoples whose prosperity makes their hearts 'proud,' Deuteronomy 8:13 and 14. Solomon, too, showed his wealth to a foreign visitor, 1 Kings 10:2 and 3, but the Queen of Sheba went away praising the LORD. In Isaiah's own book, Isaiah 2:6 and 7 speaks of a land 'full of silver and gold' and full of influences from the east, and Isaiah 30:1 to 3 and 31:1 condemn the trust in foreign help that this chapter echoes.

Babylon will then run through Scripture as the name of the proud world city, from Isaiah 13:19 and 21:9 to the cry in Revelation 18:2, 'Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great!' And the same book that foretells the exile promises the rescue, beginning with Isaiah 40:1, and the same Micah who says 'You will go to Babylon' adds 'there you will be rescued,' Micah 4:10.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The prophet-historian wants the reader to see the exile as something with a cause and not as an accident. Judah was not simply overrun because Babylon was strong. The chapter opens by recalling the illness and recovery, and that is the context for what follows: a sign of God's power became the occasion for a man to show off his own.

But he also wants the reader to see how small the causes can look. Nothing scandalous happens. Hezekiah is courteous, generous and glad. Isaiah's questions are the questions of someone who does not need to be told the answer. The point is that a heart that has just been healed and delivered can still reach for security in the wrong places, and God sees the reach.

The chapter also introduces a pattern the first hearers would know well. The prophets keep warning that Judah's leaders would rely on foreign powers and their own resources, and the exile is where that leads. Isaiah is showing his hearers that the root was already in the best king they had.

Finally, he wants the reader to hear the double message of the whole section. The king's description of the word as 'good' is hard to read. The way to be fair to the passage is to hold it as a hinge. What comes next, chapter 40, begins with 'Comfort, comfort My people.' Judgment has been spoken so that comfort can be heard against it, and not in place of it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter records what Hezekiah did and what God said would follow. It does not forbid hospitality to foreigners, diplomacy, or wealth. It cannot be used to say that every display of resources invites disaster, any more than Solomon's showing his wealth to the Queen of Sheba does, 1 Kings 10. The fault lies in the heart behind the display, as Chronicles shows: pride, and a failure to give thanks for the favour shown.

What should be carried into present life is the kind of question Isaiah asks: who are my visitors, what have I shown them, and what did I let them see about where I place my trust? Jesus says that where a person's treasure is, 'there your heart will be also,' Matthew 6:21, and Proverbs 27:2 says to let another praise you and not your own mouth.

The chapter is also descriptive in its closing words. Hezekiah's thought, 'at least there will be peace and security in my lifetime,' is reported, not recommended. It is a warning to us, and a mirror, about how easily a person can accept a hard word so long as the cost falls on someone else. The text leaves us to judge, and the pull of Scripture is to measure ourselves against what God asks, the humble walk of Micah 6:8, and not to imitate the king's reply.

debates.question: Is Hezekiah's reply in verse 8 humble acceptance or selfish relief?

views.label: Humble acceptance
views.case: He calls the word 'good,' which suggests he agrees that the LORD's judgment is right. Other kings who heard a word of judgment and humbled themselves had it deferred, as with Ahab in 1 Kings 21:27 to 29 and Josiah in 2 Kings 22:19 and 20. The mention of peace in his time is then thankful and not callous.

views.label: Selfish comfort
views.case: The narrator gives his unspoken reasoning, 'at least there will be peace and security in my lifetime,' and says nothing about his sons being taken away as eunuchs. The same man who prayed, 'remember how I have walked,' in chapter 38 here shows no grief for the future. Many readers see the passing remark as quiet complacency.

views.label: Both together
views.case: The text is deliberately ambiguous because the same heart can hold submission and self-regard. The narrator gives the thought as a reason, and the reason is what is revealing.

debates.bearing: Whichever way the verse is read, the narrator is not content to leave the reply unexamined. It asks every reader whether we are as moved by the costs that fall on later generations as by the ones that fall on us. The passage guards against both easy condemnation of Hezekiah and easy approval.

debates.question: What exactly was wrong with showing the envoys the treasures?

views.label: Pride
views.case: 2 Chronicles 32:25 names pride directly: 'his heart was proud.' The display was a boast of what he had, forgetting that it came from God, Deuteronomy 8:13 and 14.

views.label: Trust in alliances and strength
views.case: The envoys came from an enemy of Assyria, and Isaiah has been condemning reliance on foreign help throughout, Isaiah 30:1 to 3, 31:1, and 22:8 to 11. Showing the armory looks like marshalling a partnership against Assyria in place of trusting the LORD who had just destroyed Sennacherib's army.

views.label: A test he failed
views.case: Chronicles frames the visit as a test: 'God left him alone to test him,' 2 Chronicles 32:31. On this view the offence is less in a particular act than in the heart exposed when God steps back.

debates.bearing: The views are not rivals. Pride, a political calculation and a failed test can all be true of one afternoon. What the passage asks us to notice is that the visit looks harmless and the verdict does not.

debates.question: Are the 'eunuchs' of verse 7 literal, and who fulfilled the prophecy?

views.label: Literal court eunuchs in Babylon's palace
views.case: The word can mean a literal eunuch. The ancient Near East commonly used such men in royal service, and the BSB renders it 'eunuchs.' Daniel 1:3 has the king order Ashpenaz, 'the chief of his court officials,' to bring in young men of the royal family.

views.label: Court officials serving in the palace
views.case: The Hebrew word, saris, is also used for royal officials who were not necessarily castrated. On this reading the prophecy simply says that Hezekiah's descendants would serve a foreign king. Daniel and his friends fit that, though the Bible never says they were made eunuchs.

debates.bearing: The text does not require a decision. What it plainly says is that the royal line would be taken into the service of the king of Babylon, and that is what Daniel 1:1 to 7 describes. Isaiah 56:3 to 5, which speaks to the eunuch with a promise of a name 'better than that of sons and daughters,' shows that even this wound was not beyond God's reach.

study.originalLanguages:
Several small words in this chapter do large work, and one pair of words carries the whole tragedy.

Verse 2 says Hezekiah 'welcomed the envoys gladly.' The Hebrew verb is the ordinary word for being glad or rejoicing. The King James Version's 'was glad of them' keeps this. The parallel in 2 Kings 20:13 reads in that version 'hearkened unto them,' and the BSB gives 'received' there. In Isaiah the emphasis falls on delight in the visit. A king who had spent the last chapter in tears now rejoices at the first flattering attention.

The 'gift' sent with the letters is minchah, the ordinary word for a present, and also the word for tribute paid to a superior, as with Eglon in Judges 3:15. It is also the grain offering of Leviticus. The text does not tell us which sense is meant here, but the word keeps the ambiguity: a friendly gift or a bid for alliance. Either way, in the Bible a gift is rarely only that.

Verse 5 is introduced with 'Hear the word of the LORD of Hosts.' The verb is shama, 'hear,' and in the previous chapter the LORD had said to Hezekiah, 'I have heard your prayer,' Isaiah 38:5, using the same verb. The king whose prayer was heard is now commanded to hear.

The word 'carried off' in verse 6 is nasa, to lift and bear, which is the verb used of carrying a burden or taking away. Here the treasures that Hezekiah brought out for show will be lifted and borne.

Verse 7's 'eunuchs' translates saris, which is also used for a court official in general, as in the title of Ashpenaz, 'the chief of his court officials,' Daniel 1:3. The Hebrew allows either reading.

The last verse holds the pair that matters most. Hezekiah calls the word 'good,' tov, and then he thinks of 'peace and security,' shalom and emet. The BSB renders emet as 'security,' but the word normally means truth or faithfulness. In the previous chapter Hezekiah's thanksgiving used these same words, saying that those who go down to the pit cannot hope for God's 'faithfulness,' emet, 38:18 and 19, and that his anguish served his 'welfare,' shalom, 38:17. The king who sang about God's faithfulness has narrowed it into personal security for his days.

typology.type: The storehouses emptied for Babylon, verses 6 and 7
typology.fulfillment: The things Hezekiah treasured were carried to Babylon, and the temple vessels with them, Daniel 1:2 and 2 Kings 25:13 to 15. Under Cyrus they were brought back, counted out to Sheshbazzar, Ezra 1:7 to 11. The escalation in Christ is that the real treasure cannot be carried off: 'in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge,' Colossians 2:3, and an inheritance 'imperishable, undefiled, and unfading,' 1 Peter 1:4. He also gives up His own wealth on our behalf: 'though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor,' 2 Corinthians 8:9. The type falls short because the vessels were returned only as metal for a rebuilt temple; the greater temple is Christ Himself.

typology.type: Descendants taken into the palace of Babylon, verse 7
typology.fulfillment: The royal line goes into exile and the story of the Messiah's family goes with it: Matthew's genealogy marks 'fourteen from David to the exile to Babylon, and fourteen from the exile to the Christ,' Matthew 1:17. Daniel and his friends serve faithfully in the palace of a foreign king, Daniel 1:17 to 21. In Christ the exile reaches its end. He is the Son of David who comes from that broken line, and the one for whom 'there will be no end' to His government, Isaiah 9:7. The type falls short because Daniel's service was faithful but partial; it did not bring Israel home.

typology.type: Babylon as the proud world city, verses 6 and 7
typology.fulfillment: Babylon begins here as a rising power and ends in the Bible as a name for the whole proud, self-glorifying system that opposes God. Isaiah 21:9 says 'Fallen, fallen is Babylon,' and Revelation 18:2 repeats it. Nebuchadnezzar's boast, 'Is this not Babylon the Great, which I myself have built,' Daniel 4:30, shows what Hezekiah's pride was a smaller version of. In Christ the empire is judged and the city is replaced, as the book of Revelation shows. The type falls short because Babylon is a historical city and later a symbol, while the Bible's actual conflict is with the powers behind it.

typology.type: The test after the gift, 2 Chronicles 32:31
typology.fulfillment: Hezekiah was healed and then 'left alone to test him,' and he failed. Jesus, after His baptism, was tempted in the wilderness, and when the devil 'showed Him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory,' He refused to take them by compromise, Matthew 4:8 to 10. Hebrews says He 'was tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin,' Hebrews 4:15. Hezekiah displayed his treasure, apparently to court support; Christ declined the kingdoms of the world and would not leave the Father's way. The type falls short because Hezekiah's failure was real, while Christ's success is the thing that saves.

study.christ:
This chapter does not mention a coming Saviour, so its road to Christ runs through contrast and through the long story it sets in motion.

The first contrast is the display. Hezekiah showed the envoys 'everything,' and it cost his descendants. The devil once took Jesus up to a high mountain and 'showed Him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory,' Matthew 4:8. He offered them in exchange for worship, and Jesus said, 'Away from Me, Satan!' Matthew 4:10. Where a king displayed what he had to win security, the Son refused the offer of the world to remain faithful. The man who had 'nowhere to lay His head,' Matthew 8:20, had no armory to show, and the kingdom He holds cannot be carried off.

The second is the final line. Hezekiah wanted 'peace and security' in his own lifetime, shalom and emet. The New Testament says of Christ, 'He Himself is our peace,' Ephesians 2:14, and 'grace and truth came through Jesus Christ,' John 1:17, and He says, 'I am the way and the truth and the life,' John 14:6. What Hezekiah hoped to hold for his own days, Christ gives to every generation, and at His own cost. A king who was content that judgment fall on his children's generation is answered by a King who took judgment on Himself so that no later generation would have to.

The third is the line of David itself. The prophecy that Hezekiah's descendants would be carried away does not break the promise to David. Matthew shows that the line passes through the exile, and counts the Messiah as fourteen generations on from it, Matthew 1:17. 'Out of you will come forth for Me One to be ruler over Israel,' Micah 5:2, from a line that Babylon could take but not end. The Messiah is born into the exile's aftermath, as the Son sent 'when the time had fully come,' Galatians 4:4.

The last link is the book's own structure. Judgment is spoken in chapter 39, and chapter 40 opens with 'Comfort, comfort My people.' The order follows the pattern of Scripture's whole message: the word that exposes sin comes before the word that announces a remedy, and the remedy is Christ.

We should not turn Hezekiah into a picture of Jesus. He is the failing king, and the passage is more truthful for letting him fail. Christ's role in the chapter is as the one who stands at the other end of the exile.
study.god:
The passage shows a God who sees what we would prefer to leave unquestioned. Isaiah's questions are not the questions of a man gathering information. 'Where did those men come from, and what did they say to you?' and 'What have they seen in your palace?' are the questions of someone who wants Hezekiah to say aloud what he has done. This is the same God who asked 'Where are you?' in the garden, and the method is the same: He draws out a confession by asking.

He is not impressed by what impresses people. The storehouses of Judah, the gold and the armory, are counted by God as things that cannot protect and will be carried away. Yet the passage does not say that wealth is evil. In 2 Chronicles 32:29 Hezekiah's wealth is something 'God gave him.' The failure is in treating the gift as grounds for confidence. 'Let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows Me,' Jeremiah 9:23 and 24.

He is a God whose word is reliable even when it is unwelcome. Isaiah does not soften the message or alter it to suit the king's mood. The verdict of verse 6, 'Nothing will be left, says the LORD,' came true over the following century. The faithfulness of God includes His faithfulness to His warnings.

He is also the God who withholds, for a time, a judgment He has announced. The chapters before it have just shown the LORD answering a man's prayer for life. This chapter shows that even a king so favoured is not exempt from the consequences of a proud heart. Mercy and justice sit together, and neither cancels the other. The LORD does not cancel the prophecy, but He does delay it, and that delay will prove to be His patience, not His absence.

There is a hint of another truth too. The one who foretells Babylon already has plans beyond it. In the same book the LORD says of Cyrus, 'My shepherd will fulfill all that I desire,' Isaiah 44:28, and 'For your sake, I will send to Babylon,' Isaiah 43:14. A God who can announce the exile a century ahead can also announce the return. He is not surprised by the empire that takes His people.

For worship, the chapter gives us a gentle warning and a hope. We are to receive gifts gratefully without letting them become our confidence, and we are to trust a God who is both able to tell us the truth about ourselves and able to carry us through its consequences. 'God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble,' James 4:6.

crossReferences.note: The parallel account, almost identical. It spells out that the king 'received' the envoys and says that Hezekiah thought, 'Will there not at least be peace and security in my lifetime?' phrased as a question. Reading the two shows how the same sentence can be heard as relief or as resignation.

The commentary the historian adds: Hezekiah's heart was proud, he humbled himself, and God 'left him alone to test him.' This turns a seemingly small event into a test of the heart and explains why Isaiah responds so sharply.

God's word to Hezekiah in the previous chapter, 'I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears.' The king who was heard in his distress becomes the king who must hear a hard word in his comfort, and the two chapters are meant to be read as one movement.

The opening scene of the fulfilment. Nebuchadnezzar takes vessels from the house of God and young men from the royal family, who are trained for the king's service. The people named in this passage are the descendants Isaiah foresaw, and the book that follows shows how faith survives there.

The final stripping of the temple, when the Chaldeans carried to Babylon the bronze and everything of gold and silver. Isaiah's 'nothing will be left' is described here as having happened, about a century after Hezekiah's display.

Moses warns Israel that when silver and gold multiply, 'your heart will become proud, and you will forget the LORD.' It names the very danger Hezekiah faced and explains why Chronicles treats the display as a matter of the heart.

Isaiah's earlier woe on those who go for help to foreign powers and 'do not look to the Holy One of Israel.' It shows that the prophet had been preaching against this kind of trust throughout Hezekiah's reign, which is why he asks his sharp questions now.

A promise to the eunuch who keeps the LORD's covenant: 'a memorial and a name better than that of sons and daughters.' Set beside verse 7 of this chapter, it shows that even the loss of descendants in exile would be met by a place in God's house.

A prophecy from Hezekiah's own era that goes to Babylon and beyond: 'You will go to Babylon; there you will be rescued; there the LORD will redeem you.' It joins this chapter's judgment to the comfort of chapter 40 in a single verse.

Matthew organises the genealogy of Jesus into three sets of fourteen, with the exile to Babylon as the middle turning point. The exile Isaiah announces is therefore a hinge in the story of the Messiah's own family, not only in Judah's history.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's first great story of display and exile is in a garden. A man and woman reached for what was not theirs, were found out by a God who asked questions, and were sent east. Isaiah 39 is a small, grown-up version of the same story. A man with everything shows what he has, is questioned by the LORD's prophet, and learns that what he treasured will be carried east.

The chapter also answers a question the reader of the Old Testament has been carrying since Deuteronomy: how will the covenant curses actually fall? The answer is Babylon. From this point the book looks ahead to a people uprooted from the land and its king and temple, the things Genesis 12 and 2 Samuel 7 and Solomon's temple had given them. The chapters that follow will deal with what God does about that.

What the chapter sets up is the Book of Comfort. 'Comfort, comfort My people,' Isaiah 40:1, is spoken to those who inherit the consequences of this afternoon. It is given in the knowledge that the people deserved the exile and that the LORD would redeem them from it all the same. The return under Cyrus, Ezra 1, is its first fruit, with the temple vessels counted out and carried home.

But the Old Testament's return is only a partial answer. The exile, in another sense, goes on until Christ, and the genealogy at the start of the New Testament shows the line arriving 'from the exile to the Christ,' Matthew 1:17. Jesus does what Hezekiah could not. He shows the world no armory and takes none of the offered kingdoms. He lets Himself be stripped and carried off, and through that He brings His people home.

The new creation has the last word on Babylon. The city that took Judah's treasures and trained its young men to serve it falls in Revelation 18, and the treasure that was carried off is replaced by a city in which 'the glory of God' gives light, Revelation 21:23. There the kings of the earth bring their glory in, and nobody has to hide what the LORD has given or fear who sees it. The true security that Hezekiah wanted for his own days is given to the whole people of God for all ages.

quiz.q: Why did Merodach-baladan send envoys to Hezekiah?

options.text: He had heard about Hezekiah's illness and recovery.
options.note: Verse 1 states this reason directly.

options.text: He wanted to declare war on Judah.
options.note: The envoys came with letters and a gift, not a declaration of war.

options.text: He wanted to demand tribute payments.
options.note: Not the stated reason; the visit is presented as a goodwill gesture regarding Hezekiah's recovery.

options.text: He wanted to warn Hezekiah about Assyria.
options.note: The stated occasion is Hezekiah's illness and recovery, though the wider political context likely involved anti-Assyrian interests.

quiz.q: How did Hezekiah respond to the envoys' visit in verse 2?

options.text: He showed them everything in his treasure house and storehouses, holding nothing back.
options.note: Verse 2 describes exactly this complete, unrestrained display.

options.text: He refused to let them see anything of his kingdom.
options.note: The opposite; he showed them everything without exception.

options.text: He showed them only his weapons, not his wealth.
options.note: The text says he showed them silver, gold, spices, oil, and his armory, everything, not a limited selection.

options.text: He showed them a small, carefully selected portion of his wealth.
options.note: The text emphasizes there was nothing he did not show them, not a curated selection.

quiz.q: What does Isaiah prophesy will happen to Hezekiah's treasures in verses 5 to 6?

options.text: Everything in the palace and all that his fathers stored up will be carried off to Babylon.
options.note: Verse 6 states this prophecy directly, that nothing will be left.

options.text: The treasures will be safely preserved for future generations.
options.note: The opposite; the prophecy is that everything will be carried away, not preserved.

options.text: Only a small portion of the treasures will ever be lost.
options.note: The prophecy specifies that nothing will be left, not a minor loss.

options.text: The treasures will be lost to Egypt rather than Babylon.
options.note: The prophecy specifically names Babylon as the destination, not Egypt.

quiz.q: What does Isaiah say will happen to some of Hezekiah's own descendants in verse 7?

options.text: They will be taken away to serve as eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon.
options.note: Verse 7 states this directly, a foreshadowing later seen in the experience of Daniel and his companions.

options.text: They will become kings over Babylon itself.
options.note: The prophecy describes exile and servitude, not rule over Babylon.

options.text: They will remain safely in Jerusalem indefinitely.
options.note: The opposite; the prophecy specifically foretells their being taken away.

options.text: They will be given positions of honor in Assyria.
options.note: The prophecy specifically names Babylon, not Assyria, as the place of exile.

quiz.q: How does Hezekiah respond to this hard prophecy in verse 8?

options.text: He calls the LORD's word good, thinking there will at least be peace and security in his own lifetime.
options.note: Verse 8 records exactly this response, which readers have long debated as either humble or self-centered.

options.text: He immediately repents and pleads for the prophecy to be reversed.
options.note: Unlike his earlier prayer for healing, Hezekiah here accepts the word rather than pleading for its reversal.

options.text: He rejects Isaiah's prophecy as false.
options.note: The opposite; he explicitly calls the LORD's word good, accepting rather than rejecting it.

options.text: He blames the Babylonian envoys for the coming judgment.
options.note: His response is directed at accepting the LORD's word itself, not at blaming the envoys.

questions: Hezekiah showed off everything he had to impress foreign visitors. What are you tempted to display or boast about that God has actually given you as a steward, not an owner?

Isaiah's probing question, 'what have they seen in your palace,' exposed something Hezekiah had not fully considered. What question might God be asking you right now to expose a blind spot in your own life?

Hezekiah's response has been read as either humble acceptance or self-centered relief. Which do you think it was, and how do you tend to respond when consequences will fall mainly on people after you rather than on yourself?
This chapter's judgment becomes the very crisis that the Book of Comfort answers in the next chapter. Where in your life do you need to trust that God's hard words are not His last word?
The exile foretold here eventually shaped Daniel's faithful life even in a foreign court. Where might God be calling you to remain faithful even amid consequences you did not choose?

translationNotes.note: Merodach-baladan was a historical Chaldean ruler who twice seized the throne of Babylon and led resistance against Assyria, making his embassy likely more than a simple courtesy visit.
Eunuchs in ancient royal courts often held positions of significant administrative trust, so this prophecy anticipates both loss of freedom and, in figures like Daniel, real influence even in exile.

The phrase 'in my lifetime' has been read by commentators across the centuries in sharply different ways, some seeing humble resignation, others self-centered relief; the text itself leaves the king's inner motive somewhat open.
